pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Gathering, recording, classifying & presenting data

- **Standards — UK (DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires "gathering, recording, classifying and presenting data in a variety of ways to help in answering questions" and "recording findings using simple scientific language, drawings, labelled diagrams, keys, bar charts, and tables" (verbatim). The step-up from KS1 is CLASSIFYING and choosing among several PRESENTATION formats.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 4 Analyzing & Interpreting Data, grades 3–5):** the progression requires students to "represent data in tables and/or various [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-2]." Organising data into tables, bar charts and classification keys is exactly this practice at the 3–5 band.

- **Operational details:** Builds on simple recording (prerequisite mt_ZFwPZaDJ0_) and accurate measuring (mt_nUnowllzaN); shares ground with maths pictogram/table skills (mt_c29FaCTNsx). Four moves: gather, record, CLASSIFY (group by shared features, including using/making a branching KEY), and PRESENT in an appropriate format (table with headings, bar chart, pictogram, labelled diagram, key). The key ideas: a table needs clear headings; a bar chart shows how categories compare; a classification key sorts by yes/no questions about features. Feeds forward to complex graphs and to drawing conclusions (dependents mt_rDjtmDogJr, mt_7VrR1GzhrN).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). A learner who can organise data into a clearly-headed table, build a bar chart or pictogram from it, and use labelled diagrams and simple classification keys to present findings has met the bar. Line graphs, scatter graphs and scaled axes come at upper KS2 (mt_rDjtmDogJr).
bestPractices: Match the format to the data: teach that a bar chart compares categories, a table holds exact values, a key sorts things by features — so pupils CHOOSE a format for a reason rather than always drawing a bar chart.

Teach classification keys as chains of yes/no questions about observable features (does it have wings? → yes/no), and have pupils both USE a key and BUILD a simple one — building reveals why each question must split the group.
Insist on table headings and bar-chart labels/axes as the things that make a display readable by someone else — a chart without labels can't answer the question.
Connect to maths data-handling (pictograms, tables) explicitly so the science and maths skills reinforce rather than feel separate.
Keep the dataset tied to a real question so 'presenting' is communicating an answer, not decorating.
keyRepresentations: A bar chart / pictogram with labelled axes and a key
A branching classification key (yes/no questions about features)
A 'which display fits this data?' chooser (table vs bar chart vs key)
commonMisconceptions: Always defaulting to a bar chart regardless of whether the data suits it, or drawing a bar chart of individual items rather than category totals.
Omitting headings, labels or a key, making the display unreadable to anyone else.
Building a classification key with questions that don't cleanly split the group (overlapping or non-observable criteria).
Confusing classifying (grouping by feature) with simply listing.
Treating the chart as the finished goal rather than as a tool that answers the original question.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, learners gather, record, classify, and present real data using tables, bar charts/pictograms, labelled diagrams, and classification keys. The core skill is construction and format-selection: building a display that actually answers the original question, and building a key as a chain of yes/no questions about observable features, each of which must split the group. Pupils both use and build keys. Reading and choosing displays can be assessed separately, and a static exemplar chart can serve as a reference scaffold, while the primary objective remains constructing displays, not only recognising them.

activities.title: Data studio: build the table, then pick the display that reveals the answer
feedback: If you charted every individual item, notice the display is an unreadable forest and can't answer 'which is most common?' — switch to category totals and watch the tallest bar pop out.
Could a stranger read each column without you? If not, the heading is missing or mixing two kinds of information — one kind per column.

Do two groups with the same number look the same size? If bars differ in width or the scale jumps unevenly, the chart misrepresents the counts — fix equal widths and an even scale (or one fixed symbol value) first.
If you always reach for a bar chart, ask what the data needs: exact values want a table; comparing categories wants a bar chart.
activities.rationale: Presenting data is an active construction task: building the table/chart and testing whether it reveals the answer is intended to teach format-selection in a way that recognition alone does not elicit. Tying the display to a real question keeps 'presenting' about communicating an answer rather than decorating. This aligns with the stated standards for presenting data in tables and graphical displays to reveal patterns. Activity is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically requires gathering, recording, classifying and presenting data in a variety of ways, and recording findings using drawings, labelled diagrams, keys, bar charts and tables.
NGSS SEP 4 at grades 3-5 requires representing [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-1], pictographs, pie charts) to reveal patterns.
learnerActions: Start from a real question and a pile of collected data, e.g. minibeasts found in the playground, or favourite-fruit votes.
Enter the collected values into a table and decide the column headings before entering data — one kind of information per column (e.g. category | count).
Generate a bar chart or pictogram from the table and toggle between formats.

Deliberately try a poor format first: a bar for every single individual item makes an unreadable 'forest'; then switch to category totals so the tallest bar answers 'which is most common?' at a glance.
Check that two categories with the same count produce bars that look the same size, and that a pictogram uses one symbol = one fixed amount with equal intervals.
Add axis labels, a scale/key, and table headings so a stranger could read the display without you explaining it.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing the RIGHT representation is what makes data answer the question; a table holds exact values, a bar chart compares category totals, and labels/headings/scale are what make the display readable by someone else.

activities.title: Key-builder: sort creatures with yes/no feature questions
feedback: If creatures get stuck together, your question didn't split the group — rewrite it so it has a clear yes and no side.
If a group is labelled by a feeling ('scary bugs') or a preference, re-sort using a feature you can point to: legs, wings, body segments.
Could someone else sort a brand-new minibeast using your rule? If not, the criterion isn't observable or consistent enough.
Building your own key (not just using one) helps you see why each question has to divide the group — and following a ready-made key to identify a specimen is worth practising too.
activities.rationale: Both using and building a key are recommended: building is intended to reveal why each yes/no question must split the group and why criteria must be observable, addressing the misconception of sorting by subjective or overlapping categories. This supports the classifying step required by the standards. Activity is a proposed design, not a validated one.
sourceClaims: DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically requires gathering, recording, classifying and presenting data in a variety of ways, and recording findings using drawings, labelled diagrams, keys, bar charts and tables.
learnerActions: Take the same set of organisms and place a chain of yes/no questions about observable features, e.g. 'Does it have wings?', 'Does it have six legs?'
Watch the creatures funnel down the branches of the key until each one ends up alone or in a correctly sorted group.
If a question fails to split the group, notice that some creatures get stuck together — revise the question so every step divides the group.
Also practise USING a given key to identify an unknown organism, following the yes/no path.
Present the sorted groups as a labelled diagram or simple key, and state for each group the observable feature that defines it, so someone else could sort a new specimen the same way.
activities.intendedInsight: A classification key is a chain of splitting questions; every question must cleanly divide the group, and groups must be defined by features you can see — not by feelings or opinions.

activities.title: Choose and read the display (reading-side check)
feedback: If you picked a format, say why the data suits it — a reason, not habit.
When using the key, if your path leads to the wrong organism, re-read each yes/no question against the actual features you observe.
This recognition task checks reading and choosing; it does not by itself show you can construct a display, so pair it with building one.
activities.rationale: Choice, matching, and sorting formats can assess the reading/choosing side of data handling. These are recognition-style tasks, so they assess but do not elicit independent construction of a display.
learnerActions: Answer 'which chart best shows this data?' given a question and a dataset, and justify the choice (table for exact values, bar chart to compare categories, key to sort by features).
Use a given classification key to identify an organism by following the yes/no path.
Sort a set of data entries into the correct columns of a headed table.
Explain what each column of a table tells a reader, and whether equal counts appear as equal bars.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to match data to an appropriate format and read charts/keys accurately is a distinct, checkable skill that complements building displays.

activities.title: Reference: anatomy of a good chart and key (scaffold)
feedback: Use this as a checklist, then build your own display: a fixed exemplar can show the parts but cannot require you to construct one.
After consulting the reference, return to your own chart and confirm each part is present.
activities.rationale: A static labelled exemplar is a useful reference, but because the target skill is constructing displays, a fixed image is support only and should not replace building. A fixed example cannot be manipulated but can still show the parts of a good display.
learnerActions: Study a labelled exemplar bar chart and classification key, revealing the parts: headings, labelled axes, even scale/consistent symbol value, and yes/no branch questions.
Use the exemplar as a checklist when building your own table, chart, or key.
activities.intendedInsight: A well-made display has identifiable parts — headings, labels, an even scale, and cleanly splitting questions — that you can check your own work against.

constraints: Keep every dataset tied to a real question so presenting communicates an answer rather than decorating.
Build on simple recording and accurate measuring prerequisites, and connect explicitly to maths data-handling (pictograms, tables) so science and maths skills reinforce each other.

Target checkpoint is concrete/observational (Tier A): a clearly headed table, a bar chart or pictogram built from it, and labelled diagrams/simple keys. Bar charts with a simple, evenly spaced labelled scale (e.g. counting in 1s, 2s, 5s or 10s) are in scope. Line graphs and scatter graphs for presenting science findings belong to upper KS2 and are out of scope here.
Recognition-only tasks (choosing/reading a chart or key) assess the reading side but do not elicit independent construction of a display; pair them with a building task.
A static exemplar chart/key is a reference scaffold only; it cannot require the learner to construct a display.
Insist that classification groups be defined by observable features someone else could reuse, not by feelings, opinions, or preferences; and that keys use questions that cleanly split the group.
Insist on table headings and labelled bar-chart axes/scale (or a fixed pictogram symbol value) as what makes a display readable by another person.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and efficacy wording is kept to intended/may.

The interactive data-studio and key-builder examples (enter-to-table, toggle formats, key funnelling, items getting stuck) are preserved as optional interaction examples that make the learning mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory mechanisms.

One source (NGSS Appendix F, SEP 4 grades 3–5) is marked verified:false in the legacy row; its claim is retained only where it directly supports the presenting-data principle and should be re-checked.

The original 'poor fit' judgements for conversation and 3D formats were catalog fit rankings; they are not treated as universal pedagogical laws and have been dropped rather than asserted as necessity claims.

probeDeeper: What does each column in your table tell someone — could a stranger read it without you?
In your chart, do two groups with the same number look the same size? Show me.
What FEATURE did you use to make these groups? Could someone else sort a new minibeast the same way using your rule?
assess.correctAnswer: The child organises the observations into a table with appropriate column headings, builds a bar chart or pictogram with equal intervals and a consistent key/scale that shows the counts, and sorts the minibeasts into groups defined by observable features (e.g. number of legs, wings/no wings), presented as a labelled diagram or simple yes/no key.

errorPatterns.pattern: Table is disorganised — no clear headings, or categories mixed together — so it doesn't show the data clearly.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Decide the columns and their headings before entering data; one kind of information per column.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Columns lack headings or blend different kinds of information; reader can't tell what each entry means.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bar chart has unequal bar widths or gaps, or an inconsistent scale, so the bars misrepresent the counts.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix equal bar widths and an even value scale (or one symbol = one fixed amount) before drawing; check two bars with the same count look the same.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Bars vary in width or the value axis increases unevenly; a pictogram uses symbols of differing worth.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sorts by non-observable or subjective groups ('scary bugs' vs 'nice bugs') rather than by observable features.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist every group be defined by a feature you can point to — legs, wings, body segments; re-sort on an observable criterion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Group labels are feelings or opinions, not features you can see on the minibeast.

responseLevels.gap: Table lacks clear headings; chart has uneven bars or scale; groups are subjective rather than feature-based.
responseLevels.full: Organises data in a clearly headed table, builds a bar chart or pictogram with equal intervals and a consistent scale, and sorts by a stated observable feature that someone else could reuse.
responseLevels.partial: Produces a headed table and a chart, but with a scale/interval slip, or sorts on an observable feature inconsistently applied.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are the minibeasts we found in the playground and what we noticed about each one. Organise this into a clear table, make a bar chart or pictogram showing how many of each we found, and sort them into groups using a labelled diagram or a simple key. (Provide the raw observations and materials; watch how the child organises, charts, and groups.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching reveals whether grouping is by observable features or by feeling, and whether the chart uses equal intervals — things a tidy-looking result can hide. A child who understands classification sorts on a stated observable feature; a child who doesn't sorts by 'scary' versus 'nice' or by colour preference.
